item.text: {"representations":[{"case_ref":"sample_5f92088738b354c4","text":"During March 30–April 12, RMSSD fell to 22–28 ms for four consecutive days, April 3–6, from a 28-day baseline mean of 44.5 ms (43–47). It returned to 43–47 for the final six days; this local dip lowered the window mean to 39.4 ms (−12%), without a sustained decline. Resting heart rate remained 55–57 bpm, averaging 56.0 versus 56.1, despite a moderate inverse window association with RMSSD (r=−0.54). Sleep stayed near baseline: 468.5 versus 470.5 minutes, starts 22:42–22:58 and waking at 07:00. Steps averaged 8,061 versus 8,054; active minutes decreased slightly, 53.0 versus 55.4, especially on weekends (50.8 versus 53.9 weekdays). Activity began at 21:00; its association with following sleep duration was weak (r=−0.25). Low movement remained about 450 versus 448 minutes, in ten daytime bouts separated by five-minute gaps. No metrics were missing."},{"case_ref":"sample_2628ad1bc996ceaf","text":"Across March 30–April 12, sleep timing changed abruptly from baseline starts around 22:50 and fixed 07:00 waking to alternating schedules every night: seven starts at 22:07–22:16 with 06:30 waking, interleaved with seven starts at 00:37–00:44 with 09:00 waking. This persisted through the final night across weekdays and weekends. Duration remained consistent, averaging 478.2 versus the 28-day baseline of 469.7 minutes (+8.5), with little window trend. Steps averaged 8,052 versus 7,940 and trended upward; active minutes averaged 52.7 versus 54.4, rising modestly within the window and higher on weekends (55.3 versus 51.7 weekdays). Activity remained at 21:00, with essentially no association with following sleep duration (r=0.07). Low movement stayed near baseline (449 versus 452 minutes), divided into ten daytime bouts with five-minute gaps. Heart rate (56.4 versus 55.8 bpm) and RMSSD (45.0 versus 44.2 ms) changed little. No metrics were missing."},{"case_ref":"sample_291467c938997fee","text":"Sleep shifted midway through March 30–April 12: the first eight wake dates recorded 474–485 minutes, then April 7–12 recorded six consecutive shorter nights of 385–392 minutes, without recovery. Starts moved from 22:35–22:46 to 00:08–00:15 while waking stayed 07:00. Against the 28-day baseline of 470.5 minutes, the window averaged 440.6 (−30); the final six averaged 388.7, about 82 minutes below baseline, across weekdays and weekends. Activity changed from 55.6 minutes around 21:00 to six continuous 90-minute bouts at 20:30–22:00 and eight 45-minute bouts at 17:30–18:15, mostly alternating except three consecutive shorter bouts April 4–6. Both activity schedules preceded long and short sleep; the aligned association was negligible (r=−0.07). Steps (8,088 versus 7,947), interrupted low movement (449 versus 448 minutes), heart rate (56.4 versus 55.9 bpm), and RMSSD (45.7 versus 45.0 ms) remained close to baseline. No metrics were missing."},{"case_ref":"sample_bb758b54bff66927","text":"Sleep was consistently shorter throughout March 30–April 12: all 14 nights recorded 335–355 minutes versus the 28-day baseline of 455–475, averaging 346.2 versus 464.5 minutes (−118, −25%). Starts shifted approximately two hours later, from 22:45–23:05 to 00:45–01:05, while waking remained 07:00. There was only a slight upward duration trend and no return to baseline. Weekends averaged 351 minutes versus 344 weekdays, so the change persisted across both groups. Other measures remained stable: steps averaged 8,037 versus 7,983, active minutes 55.1 versus 55.6, and low movement 451.6 versus 449.9 minutes. Activity continued at 21:00; low movement comprised ten daytime bouts separated by five-minute gaps. Activity's association with following sleep duration weakened from r=−0.36 at baseline to −0.08. RMSSD stayed near 45 ms, while resting heart rate decreased slightly, 55.4 versus 56.1 bpm; their window association was negligible. No metrics were missing."}]}
